newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakh 3-mth T-bill yield may fall further-dealers.
newsitem.headline: Kazakh 3-mth T-bill yield may fall further-dealers.

text.p: Yields on Kazakh three-month Treasury bills could ease further at an auction next week, due to a lack of more attractive investment alternatives and aggressive buying by foreigners.
Kazakhstan's finance ministry is offering 650 million tenge of three-month MKM discount T-bills on Tuesday.
The yield on three-month paper fell to 17.23 percent annual on Tuesday from 18.02 percent at the previous auction on May 7. Demand was 2.22 billion tenge against 550 million on offer.
Dealers said they expected the downward trend to continue into the next week.

"The psychological barrier (of low yields) has already been passed by most banks," said Baizhan Gabdullin of Alfabank Kazakhstan, adding that his bank was already investing in repurchase operations with T-bills at just 12 percent annual.
He said local banks had a lot of money to spend and would rather invest them in T-bills than other operations.

"Where else can we invest the money? The situation is stable on the currency market because the National Bank tightly controls the tenge rate, and opeartions there are not profitable," Gabdullin said.
The tenge has been stable at around 75 per dollar since January.
Other dealers said there was little interest in investing in another instrument -- short-term notes issued by the National Bank to sterilise the money supply and keep the tenge stable.
The yield on 28-day notes fell on Wednesday to 14.59 percent annual from 17.79 percent at the previous auction on May 7.
Banks are also wary of making credits to industry, because of the risk of non-payment.

"I do not think the current trend will change next week -- the yield on three-month paper will either steady or fall further," an Agroprombank dealer said. "Banks have almost stopped financing the economy due to a large number of overdue debts on earlier credits." And foreigners -- lured by the stable tenge but entitled to buy only 15 percent of each three-month T-bill issue and 30 percent of longer-term ones -- are becoming increasingly aggressive on the government securities market.
"The participation of foreigners in T-bill auctions is another important factor -- the government is interested in attracting them and pushing down yields," Agroprombank said.
